Empirical Research Plan:  Oregon Medicaid Lottery and Labor-Market / Program-Participation Effects  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen method:  Randomized Controlled Trial (Intent-to-Treat) + Two-Stage Least Squares Instrumental‐Variables estimation.

•  Why ITT?  The lottery assignment is literally random; comparing lottery winners to losers delivers an unbiased average ITT effect of “being offered the chance to apply for Medicaid.”  
•  Why IV/2SLS?  Take-up of Medicaid is incomplete among winners and non-zero among losers.  The lottery therefore serves as a strong, externally generated instrument for actual Medicaid coverage.  A 2SLS setup recovers the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of “having Medicaid” for compliers, which is the parameter of most policy interest.

Alternative designs (DiD, RDD, event study) are unnecessary; the lottery provides cleaner, sharper exogenous variation than those quasi-experimental methods.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable (endogenous):  
  Medicaid_i = 1 if individual i is enrolled in Medicaid at survey date; 0 otherwise.

Instrument (exogenous):  
  LotteryWin_i = 1 if i’s household was randomly drawn in the 2008 Oregon reservation list; 0 otherwise.

Control group:  
  Individuals who entered the lottery but were not selected (LotteryWin_i = 0).

Treatment timing:  
  t = 0 is the date of lottery draw (March–May 2008). Outcomes are measured in follow-up surveys (~6–24 months later). Because treatment is a one-shot offer, no staggered timing complications arise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Random Assignment / Exogeneity of Instrument  
 LotteryWin is independent of unobservables that influence employment, earnings, or program take-up, conditional on pre-specified strata (e.g., household size, county) used by the state in the draw.  
 Plausibility: extremely high; verified balance tests in prior documentation.

A2. Relevance  
 Winning the lottery substantially increases Medicaid coverage (first-stage F-stat ≫ 10).  
 Plausibility: documented take-up ~25–30 pp; we will re-estimate and report F-stat.

A3. Exclusion Restriction  
 LotteryWin affects outcomes only through Medicaid coverage, not via other channels (e.g., contemporaneous information shocks).  
 Plausibility: reasonable, but potential concerns include psychological effects of winning and administrative burdens. We will probe via “placebo” outcomes and covariate controls.

A4. Monotonicity (No Defiers)  
 Nobody loses Medicaid because they won the lottery.  
 Plausibility: virtually certain—winning cannot legally revoke existing coverage.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
 No spillovers between households (households, not individuals, are lottery units).  
 Plausibility: moderate; we will cluster at household and test for geographic spillovers.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Major Threats & Mitigations  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Survey Non-Response / Attrition  
 •  Winners might respond to follow-up surveys at higher rates.  
 •  Mitigation: weight analyses by inverse-probability of response estimated from baseline data; show bounds (Lee 2009).

T2. Imperfect Exclusion (Indirect Effects)  
 •  Winning could change labor supply by reducing health-related anxiety before actual enrollment.  
 •  Mitigation: estimate “reduced-form” ITT alongside IV; if both point in same direction with similar magnitude scaled by take-up, concern abates. Include controls for post-lottery private insurance to capture substitution.

T3. Multiple Hypothesis Testing / Researcher Degrees of Freedom  
 •  Many outcomes (earnings, labor supply, SNAP, TANF, UI, etc.).  
 •  Mitigation: pre-register primary outcomes, apply family-wise error corrections (Holm-Bonferroni) or sharpened q-values.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS & IV
library(modelr)      # for randomization inference
library(sandwich)    # robust SEs

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------
lottery <- read_csv("oregon_lottery_individual.csv")   # each row = individual

# 2. Variable construction -----------------------------------------
analysis <- lottery %>%
  mutate(
    treat      = LotteryWin,                 # instrument
    medicaid   = as.numeric(EnrolledMedicaid == 1),
    employed   = as.numeric(CurrentlyEmployed == 1),
    earnings   = AnnualEarn,                 # continuous
    snap       = as.numeric(SNAP == 1),
    tanf       = as.numeric(TANF == 1),
    weight     = SurveyWeight,
    strata     = interaction(County, HHSize) # original draw strata
  )

# 3. Main specifications -------------------------------------------
# 3a. ITT: Employment
itt_emp <- feols(employed ~ treat | strata, data = analysis,
                 weights = ~weight, cluster = ~HouseholdID)
summary(itt_emp)

# 3b. 2SLS: Employment
iv_emp <- feols(employed ~ 1 | strata | medicaid ~ treat,
                data = analysis, weights = ~weight,
                cluster = ~HouseholdID)
summary(iv_emp)

# 3c. 2SLS: Earnings
iv_earn <- feols(earnings ~ 1 | strata | medicaid ~ treat,
                 data = analysis, weights = ~weight,
                 cluster = ~HouseholdID)
summary(iv_earn)

# 4. First-stage F-statistic check ---------------------------------
fs <- feols(medicaid ~ treat | strata, data = analysis,
            weights = ~weight, cluster = ~HouseholdID)
summary(fs)$iv_first_stage$F

# 5. Robustness check: covariate-adjusted IV -----------------------
iv_emp_adj <- feols(employed ~ Age + Female + PreBaselineHealth |
                    strata | medicaid ~ treat,
                    data = analysis, weights = ~weight,
                    cluster = ~HouseholdID)
summary(iv_emp_adj)

# 6. Robustness check: Lee bounds for attrition --------------------
# Example for employment
cutoff <- quantile(analysis$weight, 0.95)  # simplistic demonstration
# (Full Lee-bounds code omitted for brevity)

# 7. Randomization inference (placebo) -----------------------------
ri <- permutation_test(analysis, outcome = "employed",
                       treatment = "treat", strata = "strata",
                       reps = 1000)

print(ri$p_value)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results (Priors)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
•  Labor-market activity: Theory ambiguous.  Medicaid may reduce labor supply (fewer hours needed for employer insurance) OR improve health/productivity and increase employment.  Prior based on previous evidence: small to negligible average effect on employment (–1 pp to +1 pp).  
•  Earnings: similarly near-zero.  
•  Participation in other transfer programs: likely increases SNAP and TANF uptake by 2–5 pp because of application spillovers and reduced stigma.  
•  Aggregate economic implications: welfare improvement through risk reduction; fiscal cost partly offset by modest labor responses.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV Design)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Instrument randomly assigned (exogeneity) ...................... 1  
C2: Instrument strongly correlated with treatment (relevance) ...... 1  
C3: No direct effect of instrument beyond treatment (exclusion) .... 0  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) ..................................... 1  
C5: No interference / SUTVA ....................................... 0.5  

Overall score: 3.5 / 5 — credible but must scrutinize exclusion and spillovers.
